extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading/extraction of epistemological principles from John Locke's 'Essay concerning Human Understanding' (introductory chapters arguing against innate ideas and outlining method for investigating knowledge, belief, and assent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determined idea (definition and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: By DETERMINED, when applied to a complex idea, I mean such an one as consists of a determinate number of certain simple or less complex ideas, joined in such a proportion and situation as the mind has before its view, and sees in itself, when that idea is present in it, or should be present in it, when a man gives a name to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When any one uses any term, he may have in his mind a determined idea which he makes it the sign of, and to which he should keep it steadily annexed during that present discourse. The want of this is the cause of no small obscurity and confusion in men’s thoughts and discourses. Determined ideas are less liable to mistakes than vague 'clear and distinct' language; having such determined ideas will end many doubts and disputes that depend on the doubtful and uncertain use of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep names steadily annexed to precise ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: That this idea, thus determined, i.e. which the mind has in itself, and knows, and sees there, be determined without any change to that name, and that name determined to that precise idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If men had such determined ideas in their inquiries and discourses, they would both discern how far their own inquiries and discourses went, and avoid the greatest part of the disputes and wranglings they have with others. Anti-pattern: using names without keeping them linked to a precise idea produces obscurity and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary aim of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: To inquire into the original, certainty, and extent of HUMAN KNOWLEDGE, together with the grounds and degrees of BELIEF, OPINION, and ASSENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explicitly excludes physical/metaphysical hypotheses about the essence of mind or the mechanics of sensation; the investigation is limited to how discerning faculties attain notions, the certainty of knowledge, and the grounds of assent versus opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part method for investigating understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: First, inquire into the original of those ideas which a man observes and is conscious to himself he has in his mind. Secondly, show what knowledge the understanding hath by those ideas and the certainty, evidence, and extent of it. Thirdly, inquire into the nature and grounds of FAITH or OPINION and the reasons and degrees of ASSENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Locke's explicit research plan: origin → scope/evidence of knowledge → nature/grounds of assent; use this method to separate knowledge from opinion and to evaluate certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the bounds between opinion and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: It is therefore worth while to search out the bounds between opinion and knowledge; and examine by what measures, in things whereof we have no certain knowledge, we ought to regulate our assent and moderate our persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion: regulate assent according to available measures of certainty; avoid demanding demonstration where probability suffices for conduct. Anti-pattern: insisting on certainty where only probability is attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the powers and limits of the understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: If by this inquiry into the nature of the understanding, I can discover the powers thereof; how far they reach; to what things they are in any degree proportionate; and where they fail us, I suppose it may be of use to prevail with the busy mind of man to be more cautious in meddling with things exceeding its comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic humility: identify what our faculties are suited for and stop when at the utmost extent of their tether. Anti-pattern: extending inquiry beyond capacities, raising insoluble disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses → memory → abstraction (origin of ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The senses at first let in PARTICULAR ideas, and furnish the yet empty cabinet, and the mind by degrees growing familiar with some of them, they are lodged in the memory, and names got to them. Afterwards, the mind proceeding further, abstracts them, and by degrees learns the use of general names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account of how ideas are acquired: particular sensory input becomes stored, then abstraction produces general ideas and language; this process undercuts claims of innate specific ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal consent does not prove innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: This argument, drawn from universal consent, has this misfortune in it, that if it were true in matter of fact, that there were certain truths wherein all mankind agreed, it would not prove them innate, if there can be any other way shown how men may come to that universal agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke objects to the 'universal consent' argument for innate ideas, noting (1) many (children, idiots, savages) do not know such principles, and (2) even if universal assent existed, alternative explanations (acquisition) could account for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of awareness in children/idiots refutes imprinting claim
rubrics_metrics.description: For, first, it is evident, that all children and idiots have not the least apprehension or thought of them. And the want of that is enough to destroy that universal assent which must needs be the necessary concomitant of all innate truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a principle were truly imprinted from birth it ought to be perceived; the fact that some minds never perceive these supposed innate maxims is evidence against innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coming to use of reason is not evidence of innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually answered, that all men know and assent to them, WHEN THEY COME TO THE USE OF REASON; and this is enough to prove them innate. ... I deny that the coming to the use of reason is the precise time when they are first taken notice of; and if that were the precise time, I deny that it would prove them innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two possible senses of the claim are refuted: (a) that reason 'reveals' innate truths (but reason deduces from known principles), and (b) that the timing of discovery (when reason arrives) shows innateness — both are inadequate to establish innate impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready assent on first hearing is not a mark of innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Since men never fail after they have once understood the words, to acknowledge them for undoubted truths, they would infer, that certainly these propositions were first lodged in the understanding. ... If ready assent at first hearing were a mark of innate, then many numerical and simple empirical propositions would be innate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that immediate assent upon understanding a proposition demonstrates self-evidence given clear ideas, not innateness. Anti-pattern: conflating self-evidence or immediacy of assent with being native/imprinted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-evidence depends on having clear and distinct ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A child knows not that three and four are equal to seven, till he comes to be able to count seven, and has got the name and idea of equality; and then, upon explaining those words, he presently assents to, or rather perceives the truth of that proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for assent: understanding the terms and having the relevant ideas in mind produces immediate assent; so clarity of ideas explains why some propositions are self-evident when proposed and understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason is deduction from known principles (cannot make innate truths)
rubrics_metrics.description: How can these men think the use of reason necessary to discover principles that are supposed innate, when reason (if we may believe them) is nothing else but the faculty of deducing unknown truths from principles or propositions that are already known?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If knowledge truly were innate, it should not require the use of reason to be discovered; the fact that reason is invoked to 'discover' these principles supports the acquired-origin view rather than innate-imprint.
